blocks.text: 1. What Is an OOD Interview?

An object oriented design interview hands you a vague, real world thing, a parking lot, a vending machine, an ATM, and asks you to turn it into clean, working classes. There is no single correct answer and no hidden algorithm. You are judged on how you think, structure, and communicate.

metadata.alt: The OOD journey: from a vague problem to clean working code

blocks.text: The journey is always the same shape: understand the problem, find the objects hiding in it, connect them with the right relationships, apply a pattern where it genuinely fits, and write code that a teammate could extend tomorrow. Every topic in this course trains one part of that journey.
OOD interviews do not test whether you know the answer. They test whether you can design one.

blocks.text: 2. How It Differs From Other Interviews
blocks.content: 2. How It Differs From Other Interviews

blocks.text: Candidates often prepare for the wrong round, so know exactly what this one is. The three technical interview types reward different skills.

metadata.alt: DSA, OOD, and system design rounds reward different skills

items: DSA round: one correct, efficient algorithm; the code is small and the answer is checkable
OOD round: a set of classes with clear responsibilities; the answer is a design that survives change
System design round: servers, databases, and queues at scale; boxes and arrows, little code

blocks.text: OOD sits in the middle: more code than system design, more structure than DSA. It is the round that most closely mirrors day to day software engineering, which is exactly why companies love it for mid and senior levels.
3. What Interviewers Actually Evaluate
The rubric behind the interview is remarkably consistent across companies. Five signals decide the outcome.

items: Requirement clarification: did you scope the problem before designing, or dive in blind?
Object modelling: do your classes map to real concepts, each with one responsibility?
Pattern judgement: did you apply a pattern because it fits, and can you say why?
Code quality: is the code you write clean, compiling in your head, and honest about what is stubbed?
Edge cases and communication: did you name the failure paths out loud before being asked?

blocks.text: An unjustified pattern name is a red flag. A justified simple design is a green one.
blocks.content: An unjustified pattern name is a red flag. A justified simple design is a green one.

blocks.text: 4. The Four Pillars You Must Own
blocks.content: 4. The Four Pillars You Must Own

blocks.text: Everything in OOD stands on four fundamentals. You will not be asked to define them, you will be watched using them.

metadata.alt: The four pillars of object oriented programming

blocks.text: 4.1 Encapsulation
Data hides behind methods that guard it. A ParkingSpot does not expose an occupied flag for anyone to flip; it offers tryOccupy() which enforces the rules.

codes.python:
import threading


class ParkingSpot:
    def __init__(self):
        self._occupied = False              # hidden state
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def try_occupy(self) -> bool:           # the only door in
        with self._lock:
            if self._occupied:
                return False
            self._occupied = True
            return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    spot = ParkingSpot()
    print(spot.try_occupy())  # True
    print(spot.try_occupy())  # False

blocks.text: 4.2 Abstraction
Callers see what a thing does, never how. The vending machine calls pay(amount) and has no idea whether cash was counted or a card gateway was called.
4.3 Inheritance
Shared behaviour lives once in a base type. Bike, Car, and Truck extend Vehicle so the parking flow handles all three through one reference. Use it for true is a relationships only.
4.4 Polymorphism

One call, many behaviours. machine.state.selectItem() does something completely different in IdleState and HasMoneyState, and the machine never needs to check which is which. This single idea powers the State and Strategy patterns.
5. Relationships Between Objects
Interviewers listen for whether you know who owns whom. Four relationships cover everything, and choosing the right one is a scored moment.

metadata.alt: The four relationships with a real example of each

items: Composition: strong ownership, lifecycles tied. A ParkingFloor cannot exist without its ParkingLot
Aggregation: holds but does not own. A shelf holds an Item, but the item definition outlives the shelf
Association: uses without holding. The ATM calls BankService but owns nothing inside it
Inheritance: is a kind of. A Car is a Vehicle, so it flows through every Vehicle code path

blocks.text: The quick test: if the owner dies, does the part die too? Yes means composition. Does it merely hold a reference? Aggregation. Does it just call it? Association.
6. Interfaces vs Abstract Classes
This is one of the most common follow up questions, so have the answer ready. Both define contracts, but they solve different problems.

items: Interface: a pure capability with no state. Use it when unrelated classes must answer the same calls, like State or PaymentStrategy
Abstract class: a partial implementation with shared fields. Use it when children share real code and data, like NoteHandler holding the note count and the chain link

blocks.text: Interface for a contract, abstract class for a shared skeleton. Say that sentence and the follow up is done.

blocks.text: 7. SOLID: The Principles That Score
SOLID is not theory in this round, it is the checklist your design is graded against. Learn to name the principle at the moment you apply it.

metadata.alt: The five SOLID principles in one view

items: Single Responsibility: each class has one reason to change; the dispenser moves cash and nothing else
Open Closed: new behaviour arrives as new classes; a new payment method touches zero existing files
Liskov Substitution: any subtype drops in cleanly; every ATMState works wherever a State is expected
Interface Segregation: many small interfaces beat one fat one; State has four methods, not forty
Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions; the ATM holds a BankService interface, never a concrete bank

blocks.text: The habit worth building: when you make a choice in the interview, attach the principle. "I am keeping pricing behind an interface so the lot is closed against pricing changes" scores twice, once for the design and once for the reasoning.
8. The Patterns You Will Actually Use
blocks.content: 8. The Patterns You Will Actually Use

blocks.text: Five patterns cover almost every classic OOD problem. Learn these deeply instead of memorising twenty superficially.

metadata.alt: The five workhorse patterns and where each one earns its place

items: State: behaviour changes by mode. The vending machine and the ATM session are the textbook cases
Strategy: a swappable policy behind an interface. Parking pricing, spot allocation, payment methods
Factory: centralised construction of a family. Creating the right Vehicle subclass from a type code
Observer: many listeners react to events. Displays, receipt printers, telemetry
Chain of Responsibility: a request cascades through handlers. ATM note cassettes splitting an amount

blocks.text: Singleton deserves one honest sentence: it appears in every book, but in interviews prefer saying "one instance managed by dependency injection", because singletons complicate testing and the interviewer knows it.
9. The Classic Problems and Their Shapes
blocks.content: 9. The Classic Problems and Their Shapes

blocks.text: Most OOD questions are one of a dozen classics, and each has a known shape. Recognising the shape in the first minute is half the interview.

metadata.alt: The classic problems and the design shape at the heart of each

items: Parking Lot: entities plus swappable policies, with one atomic contention point per spot
Vending Machine: the State pattern, money handling, and inventory
ATM: State for the session plus Chain of Responsibility for notes, with a strict money ordering
Chess or Snake and Ladder: a board, piece inheritance, and a rules engine validating moves
Splitwise: balances as a graph and split strategies per expense type
Elevator: State plus a scheduling strategy deciding which car answers a call

blocks.text: This course walks each classic with the full template: requirements, entities, UML, patterns with justification, sequence diagrams, working Java, concurrency, and the follow ups interviewers actually ask.
10. Mistakes That Fail Candidates
The same handful of mistakes sink most attempts. Every one of them is avoidable with awareness.

items: Diving into code in the first minute: skipping clarification is the loudest red flag there is
The god class: one Machine class doing inventory, money, and state in five hundred lines
Pattern name dropping: announcing Factory and Observer with no problem that needs them
Boolean flag state machines: hasMoney and itemSelected flags instead of state classes
Ignoring failure paths: designing only the happy path until the interviewer forces the issue
Silent typing: writing code without narrating intent, leaving the interviewer nothing to score

blocks.text: The interviewer can only give you points for what they hear. Think out loud, always.

blocks.text: 11. How to Prepare With This Course
blocks.content: 11. How to Prepare With This Course

blocks.text: Preparation is a path, not a pile. Follow it in order and each stage compounds the last.

metadata.alt: The preparation path: framework, classics, timed practice, mocks

items: Learn the framework first: the next guide gives you a repeatable seven step method for any problem
Study the classics deeply: Parking Lot, Vending Machine, and ATM teach the shapes everything else reuses
Practise out loud with a timer: forty five minutes, whiteboard or editor, narrating every decision
Mock interviews: a friend or a mirror; the speaking muscle is trained, not assumed
